Leviticus 1.audience: These instructions are spoken from the newly built tabernacle (Leviticus 1:1) to ordinary Israelites who brought offerings, and they describe what each worshipper did with his own hands: laying a hand on the animal's head and killing it before the LORD.

culture.title: Offerings by wealth
culture.text: A burnt offering could be a bull, a sheep or goat, or birds. Turtledoves and young pigeons allowed poorer families to offer what they could afford, as Mary and Joseph did after Jesus' birth (Luke 2:24).

culture.title: Sacrifice across the ancient world
culture.text: Animal sacrifice was practiced by nearly every ancient people. Many believed the gods ate the offerings; Israel's psalms deny that God needs food (Psalm 50:12–13).

Leviticus 2.audience: Grain offerings came from the produce of Israel's own fields. Hearers knew the ingredients—fine flour, olive oil, and frankincense—from daily life and worship.

culture.title: Ways of baking
culture.text: The chapter lists the ways bread was cooked: baked in an oven, on a flat griddle (pan), or in a deep pan (frying pan). These were the ordinary methods of an Israelite kitchen.

culture.title: Salt of the covenant
culture.text: Salt preserved food and was shared at meals that sealed agreements. Every offering was to be seasoned with "the salt of the covenant."

culture.title: No leaven or honey
culture.text: Leaven and honey both ferment. They could be brought as firstfruits but were not to be burned on the altar.

Leviticus 3.audience: The peace offering was the one most Israelites shared in, because most of the animal was eaten by the worshipper and his family in a festive meal (Leviticus 7:15–16).

culture.title: The fat
culture.text: The fat around the internal organs was considered the best part and was burned for the LORD. Israelites were forbidden to eat this fat or blood.

culture.title: Fat-tailed sheep
culture.text: The sheep of the region have broad, fatty tails. The whole rump fat, cut off "hard by the backbone," was part of the offering.

Leviticus 4.audience: The law addresses four kinds of people separately: the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler, and an ordinary person (Leviticus 4:3, 13, 22, 27). Each brought a different offering for sins committed unknowingly.

culture.title: Rank and responsibility
culture.text: The priest's sin required a bull, the most costly animal, because his sin brought guilt on the people. A ruler brought a male goat and an ordinary person a female goat or lamb.

culture.title: Burning outside the camp
culture.text: The remains of the priest's sin offering were burned in a clean place outside the camp. Hebrews refers to this practice (Hebrews 13:11–12).

Leviticus 5.audience: These rules covered common situations in village life: failing to testify, touching something unclean, or making a rash oath. Every Israelite could find himself in one of them.

culture.title: Offerings for the poor
culture.text: Someone who could not afford a lamb brought two birds, and someone who could not afford birds brought a tenth of an ephah of flour. No one was excluded because of poverty.

culture.title: Restitution plus a fifth
culture.text: Wrong done to holy things had to be repaid in full with a fifth added. The same rule applies to wrongs against a neighbor (Leviticus 6:5).

Leviticus 6.audience: From Leviticus 6:8 the instructions turn to the priests—"Command Aaron and his sons"—and explain how they handled each offering.

culture.title: Perpetual fire
culture.text: The altar fire was never to go out. Priests added wood every morning and removed the ashes in linen garments.

culture.title: Holy food for priests
culture.text: Priests had no land of their own; part of many offerings became their food, eaten in the holy place.

Leviticus 7.audience: The chapter sets out which portions belonged to the priests: the breast and the right shoulder of the peace offering (Leviticus 7:31–34). Israelites bringing offerings knew what would be given to the priest.

culture.title: Eating on the same day
culture.text: Without refrigeration, meat spoiled quickly in the heat. Thanksgiving offerings had to be eaten the same day, and other peace offerings by the second day.

culture.title: The wave offering
culture.text: The breast was "waved" before the LORD—lifted and presented—and then given to Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 7:31).

Leviticus 8.audience: This chapter carries out the instructions given in Exodus 29. Israel's priests traced their consecration to this seven-day ceremony at the door of the tabernacle.

culture.title: Investiture
culture.text: Officials in the ancient world were installed by being dressed in garments of office. Moses clothes Aaron in the coat, girdle, robe, ephod, breastplate, and mitre.

culture.title: Seven days
culture.text: The priests stayed at the tabernacle door for seven days of ordination. Seven-day periods recur in Israel's rituals of purification and dedication.

Leviticus 9.audience: Israel's priests began their service on the eighth day (Leviticus 9:1). Hearers would see the whole congregation present for the first sacrifices offered by Aaron.

culture.title: Fire from the LORD
culture.text: Fire came out and consumed the offering, and the people shouted and fell on their faces. A similar sign marked the dedication of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 7:1–3).

culture.title: The priestly blessing
culture.text: Aaron lifts his hands toward the people and blesses them. The words of the priestly blessing are given in Numbers 6:24–26.

Leviticus 10.audience: Israel's priests learned from this chapter that serving God was not to be done carelessly. Moses' words, "I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me" (Leviticus 10:3), stood as a warning to every priest after them.

culture.title: Censers
culture.text: A censer was a pan for carrying burning coals, on which incense was placed. Nadab and Abihu offer "strange fire" not commanded by the LORD.

culture.title: Mourning customs
culture.text: Mourners normally let their hair hang loose and tore their clothes. Aaron and his remaining sons are told not to do so while serving.

culture.title: No wine on duty
culture.text: Priests were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink before entering the tabernacle, so that they could tell holy from common.

Leviticus 11.audience: These food laws set Israel apart in everyday eating. Hearers lived with them at every meal; Peter, centuries later, still said he had "never eaten any thing that is common or unclean" (Acts 10:14).

culture.title: Clean and unclean animals
culture.text: Land animals had to both chew the cud and have split hooves—like cattle, sheep, and goats. The pig, widely eaten by some neighbors, was forbidden.

culture.title: Water creatures
culture.text: Only water creatures with fins and scales were clean. Shellfish and eels were excluded.

Leviticus 12.audience: Every Israelite family knew these rules after childbirth. Mary kept them after Jesus' birth, bringing the poor family's offering of two birds (Luke 2:22–24).

culture.title: Purification after birth
culture.text: A mother was ritually unclean for a period after giving birth—forty days for a son and eighty for a daughter—and did not enter the sanctuary. At the end she brought a burnt offering and a sin offering (Leviticus 12:6).

Leviticus 13.audience: Priests were the public health officers of Israel's camp and towns. This chapter tells them how to examine skin conditions and decide who must live outside the camp.

culture.title: "Leprosy" in the Bible
culture.text: The Hebrew word covers a range of skin diseases, and even mold in fabric (Leviticus 13:47), not only the illness now called leprosy (Hansen's disease).

culture.title: Isolation
culture.text: A person with the disease wore torn clothes, left the hair loose, covered the upper lip, and called out "Unclean, unclean," living alone outside the camp. The lepers who met Jesus stood "afar off" (Luke 17:12).

Leviticus 14.audience: Israelites restored from skin disease went through this ceremony. Jesus told the healed leper to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Mark 1:44).

culture.title: Cedar, scarlet, and hyssop
culture.text: Cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop—a small, bushy plant—were used in purification rites. Hyssop was used to sprinkle blood or water (Exodus 12:22; Psalm 51:7).

culture.title: Mold in houses
culture.text: Stone and mud-brick houses could develop mold or mildew. Infected stones were removed and the walls scraped and replastered.

Leviticus 15.audience: These laws concerned the private lives of every Israelite household. Their stated purpose was to keep uncleanness away from the tabernacle in the camp (Leviticus 15:31).

culture.title: Washing with running water
culture.text: Running ("living") water from a spring or stream was used for cleansing. Bathing and washing clothes ended most forms of uncleanness at evening.

culture.title: Earthen and wooden vessels
culture.text: Clay pots are porous and could not be fully cleaned, so they were broken; wooden vessels could be rinsed.

Leviticus 16.audience: This was the most solemn day of Israel's year, when the whole people fasted and did no work. It is still kept in Judaism as Yom Kippur, and Hebrews 9:7 recalls the high priest going in "once every year."

culture.title: The scapegoat
culture.text: The high priest laid both hands on a live goat, confessed the people's sins over it, and sent it into the wilderness. The KJV's "scapegoat" translates the Hebrew "Azazel."

culture.title: Linen garments
culture.text: On this day the high priest set aside his gold and colored garments and wore plain white linen when entering the most holy place.

Leviticus 17.audience: This chapter addresses both Israelites and "the strangers which sojourn among you" (Leviticus 17:10). The rule against eating blood applied to everyone living in Israel's camp.

culture.title: Sacrifices in the field
culture.text: People in the ancient world offered sacrifices in open country to spirits or demons. The KJV's "devils" translates a word meaning ‘goats’ or goat-demons.

culture.title: Draining blood
culture.text: A hunter had to pour out the blood of game and cover it with dirt. Later Jewish practice of kosher slaughter grew from this rule.

Leviticus 18.audience: The laws begin by naming the practices of Egypt, where Israel had lived, and Canaan, where they were going (Leviticus 18:3). Hearers were told not to live like either.

culture.title: Molech
culture.text: Molech was a god associated with child sacrifice. Later kings of Judah burned their children in the valley of Hinnom (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35).

culture.title: Close-kin marriage
culture.text: Royal families in Egypt sometimes married close relatives, including siblings. Israel's law forbade marriage within close family degrees.

Leviticus 19.audience: This chapter is addressed to "all the congregation of the children of Israel" (Leviticus 19:2), not just priests. It joins worship with care for neighbors, workers, the deaf, the blind, and strangers.

culture.title: Gleaning
culture.text: Farmers left the corners of their fields unharvested and did not go back for dropped grain or grapes. The poor and strangers could gather it—exactly what Ruth does in Boaz's field (Ruth 2:2–3).

culture.title: Mourning practices
culture.text: Shaving the head or beard in certain ways and cutting the skin were mourning rites among Israel's neighbors. The prophets of Baal cut themselves at Carmel (1 Kings 18:28).

culture.title: Honest weights
culture.text: Merchants weighed goods with stones on a balance. Dishonest traders kept one set of weights for buying and another for selling.

Leviticus 20.audience: These penalties were to be carried out by "the people of the land" (Leviticus 20:2)—the community as a whole—showing that Israel's holiness was a shared responsibility.

culture.title: Mediums and wizards
culture.text: Consulting the dead through a medium was common in the ancient Near East. King Saul later did so at Endor despite having banned it (1 Samuel 28:7–9).

Leviticus 21.audience: These rules were for Israel's priests, the sons of Aaron, and especially the high priest. Ordinary Israelites would see their priests held to a higher standard.

culture.title: Contact with the dead
culture.text: Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days. Priests could do so only for close family; the high priest not even for them (Leviticus 21:11).

culture.title: Physical blemishes
culture.text: A priest with a physical defect could eat the holy food but could not serve at the altar, just as a blemished animal could not be offered.

Leviticus 22.audience: Both priests and worshippers are addressed: priests on eating holy food, and Israelites and strangers on the quality of the animals they offered.

culture.title: Blemished offerings
culture.text: Animals offered had to be without defect. Malachi later rebukes priests for accepting blind, lame, and sick animals (Malachi 1:8).

culture.title: Seven days with the mother
culture.text: A newborn calf, lamb, or kid was to stay with its mother seven days before it could be offered.

Leviticus 23.audience: This is Israel's calendar of holy days. Hearers kept these feasts year after year; the Gospels and Acts are set around several of them (John 7:2; Acts 2:1).

culture.title: Firstfruits and Pentecost
culture.text: The first sheaf of barley was waved before the LORD, and fifty days later the feast of weeks celebrated the wheat harvest. In Greek, this feast was called Pentecost, ‘fiftieth.’

culture.title: Living in booths
culture.text: During the feast of tabernacles, families lived for seven days in shelters made of branches, recalling the wilderness journey.

culture.title: Trumpets
culture.text: The first day of the seventh month was a day of blowing trumpets. In later Jewish practice it became Rosh Hashanah, the new year.

Leviticus 24.audience: The case in this chapter involves the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father (Leviticus 24:10). The ruling makes clear that one law applied to stranger and Israelite alike (Leviticus 24:22).

culture.title: Lamps and loaves
culture.text: Olive oil was brought by the people to keep the lamps burning continually, and twelve loaves were set out each Sabbath. These were ongoing contributions from the whole community.

culture.title: Stoning outside the camp
culture.text: Executions took place outside the camp, and witnesses laid their hands on the guilty person's head before the community carried out the sentence.

Leviticus 25.audience: These laws assumed an agricultural people settled in their own land. Hearers knew that land was held by families, and that poverty could force a family to sell land or even themselves into service.

culture.title: The jubilee
culture.text: Every fiftieth year, land returned to its original family and Israelite servants went free. "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land" is inscribed on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.

culture.title: Redeeming land
culture.text: A close relative had the right and duty to buy back land sold by a poor family member. This is the custom behind Boaz's actions in Ruth 4.

culture.title: No interest to the poor
culture.text: Israelites were forbidden to charge interest to a poor fellow Israelite. Loans in that world were usually for survival, not business.

Leviticus 26.audience: Israel later read its exile in Babylon in light of these warnings, when the land at last enjoyed "her sabbaths" (2 Chronicles 36:21). Hearers knew both the gift of good harvests and the fear of drought and war.

culture.title: Treaty blessings and curses
culture.text: Ancient treaties ended with lists of blessings for keeping the agreement and curses for breaking it. Leviticus 26 follows the same pattern.

culture.title: Rain in season
culture.text: Canaan depended on autumn and spring rains. Drought meant failed crops and famine.

Leviticus 27.audience: Israelites made vows to the LORD in times of trouble or gratitude. This chapter sets the values for redeeming what was vowed—persons, animals, houses, and fields.

culture.title: Valuing persons
culture.text: A person dedicated by vow could be redeemed by paying a set amount of silver, ranging from fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty down to three shekels for a girl under five.

culture.title: The tithe
culture.text: A tenth of all crops and herds belonged to the LORD. Animals were counted as they passed "under the rod" of the shepherd, and every tenth one was set apart.
